passed.title: Python ints infer as Int64, so cs.unsigned_integer() can silently match nothing
passed.trap: `cs.unsigned_integer` selects by dtype, not by value. A column of non-negative Python ints is inferred as `pl.Int64`, so it is never selected. When nothing matches, `DataFrame.select` returns an empty frame instead of raising an error. If you want unsigned columns, declare them with `schema_overrides` (or cast them), and check what matched before you rely on it.
passed.example:
import polars as pl
import polars.selectors as cs

df = pl.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2], "b": [3, 4]})
print(df.schema)
print(df.select(cs.unsigned_integer()).columns)

df2 = pl.DataFrame(
    {"a": [1, 2], "b": [3, 4]},
    schema_overrides={"a": pl.UInt32},
)
print(df2.select(cs.unsigned_integer()).columns)

passed.title: ~cs.unsigned_integer() means every other column, not the signed integers
passed.trap: `~cs.unsigned_integer()` takes the complement over all columns. The result includes strings, floats, dates and so on, not just signed integers. Code that then applies integer math to that selection can fail or touch the wrong columns. Use `cs.signed_integer()` for signed integers, or the set difference `cs.integer() - cs.unsigned_integer()`.
passed.example:
import polars as pl
import polars.selectors as cs

df = pl.DataFrame(
    {"foo": [-1, -2], "bar": [3, 4], "zap": ["ab", "cd"]},
    schema_overrides={"bar": pl.UInt32},
)
print(df.select(~cs.unsigned_integer()).columns)
print(df.select(cs.signed_integer()).columns)
print(df.select(cs.integer() - cs.unsigned_integer()).columns)

passed.title: pl.col(pl.UInt32) matches one width; cs.unsigned_integer() matches all unsigned widths
passed.trap: Selecting by a single dtype, such as `pl.col(pl.UInt32)`, only picks columns of exactly that dtype. `UInt8`, `UInt16` and `UInt64` columns are silently left out. If you mean every unsigned integer column, use `cs.unsigned_integer()`, which covers all of these unsigned widths.
passed.example:
import polars as pl
import polars.selectors as cs

df = pl.DataFrame(
    {"small": [1, 2], "bar": [3, 4], "baz": [5, 6]},
    schema_overrides={"small": pl.UInt8, "bar": pl.UInt32, "baz": pl.UInt64},
)
print(df.select(pl.col(pl.UInt32)).columns)
print(df.select(cs.unsigned_integer()).columns)

note.title: Casting negative values to an unsigned dtype fails under the default strict cast
note.trap: A common move is to cast columns to an unsigned type so that `cs.unsigned_integer()` picks them up. With the default `strict=True`, `Expr.cast` raises an error if any value cannot be represented, such as a negative number. Passing `strict=False` turns those values into null instead of raising. Choose the behaviour you want on purpose, and check null counts after a non-strict cast.
note.example:
import polars as pl
import polars.selectors as cs

df = pl.DataFrame({"x": [-1, 5]})
try:
    df.with_columns(pl.col("x").cast(pl.UInt32))
except Exception as e:
    print(type(e))

out = df.with_columns(pl.col("x").cast(pl.UInt32, strict=False))
print(out.select(cs.unsigned_integer()))
print(out.null_count())

note.title: Call the selector: cs.unsigned_integer() needs parentheses
note.trap: `cs.unsigned_integer` is a function that returns a selector. If you pass the bare function object to `DataFrame.select`, it is not treated as a column selection and the call fails. Write `df.select(cs.unsigned_integer())` instead.
note.example:

import polars.selectors as cs

df = pl.DataFrame(
    {"bar": [3, 4], "zap": ["ab", "cd"]},
    schema_overrides={"bar": pl.UInt32},
)
try:
    df.select(cs.unsigned_integer)
except Exception as e:

print(df.select(cs.unsigned_integer()).columns)
